texto: This feels like one of those movies that is purposely vague in key ways to allow the audience to imprint onto it, and that kind of film is never going to work for me. At its core, we have a father and daughter on vacation together. There are moments where they bond. There is obvious childhood tragedy for the father, which is probably why he seems to drink a lot, yet he's not one of those abusive drunks, so it's ok? We're never really given much depth beyond that. It's a girl growing up, having a first kiss, hanging with other kids on vacation. It's nice that there isn't any kind of bullying or any other overtly negative elements that usually make up these narratives. It's mostly just moments shared between father and daughter, mostly bonding. At the same time, not much actually happens for the entire runtime. There seems to be implied longing, but again, the narrative is kept vague on purpose so that we can somehow imprint on it. The thing is, I am not watching a movie to do its job for it. If there isn't much story there, I'm not going to fill in the blanks for it. If I want to do that, I will either work on one of my own stories or read a book. Is this supposed to be sad and reflective? I never got to vacation with my father before he died when I was around 8 or 9, I never got these moments with him... and to have it be such a positive experience... this girl is fortunate. All I know is real tragedy related to my father. Did the girl's father die right after this? Or was it years later? We see her as an adult, all reflecting and shit, but as I said, things are left mostly vague, so who knows? At least she has cherished moments with her father. More than a lot of us got. On top of that, I think people confuse realism for good. Yeah, it is shot very realistically, the performances are very natural, yet story wise, there isn't much there, and I really dislike the way this was shot, which is probably one of the main sticking points for me. Often badly framed, or where it often focuses on 'experiencing', rather than what they are experiencing, so for instance, they are playing pool, we see them take the shot, but not any of what's actually happening in the game. Or another instance, they play an arcade game, but we never really see what they are playing. As for the bad framing, at times people are talking and the frame is like whatever. Or like, the scene where there is a TV, a mirror behind it, and the whole scene is either shot from a camcorder feeding to the TV or later, when the camcorder is off, what we barely see in the reflection on the screen or in the fragment of exposed mirror is all we get. It is certainly a choice. Oh, I get it, being so 'artistic' in its reflection on what's happening with the character, but it goes on for too long and it's just badly framed, all of it. Or this repeated cutting to a dance club, flashing lights, to show this reoccurring element of the father dancing... but mostly, it is just hard to see anything. Too much of the film is like this. Extended scenes of someone laying around, or badly framed shots like this that are clearly intended to be artistic, but end up being that in a bad way. I remember reading positive comments about this film and it sounds like it should be a good one, right? I expect a level of crudeness from a documentary, because it is trying to capture something in a moment and bring it all together, but when it's a narrative film that looks mostly like a badly shot documentary, that seems to have less story than many documentaries... what are we even doing here?

texto: J'ai trouvé le film très lent et il manque, selon moi, de dynamisme. Pendant une grande partie du film, j'ai eu du mal à être réellement captivé, la seule scène qui m'a vraiment marqué est la séquence finale, lorsque le père et sa fille dansent ensemble avant la fin de leurs vacances. Les flashbacks qui s'entremêlent à ce moment donnent enfin tout son sens au film et apportent une forte charge émotionnelle. Le film montre avec beaucoup de subtilité comment le père cache sa souffrance pour préserver sa fille. En apparence, il essaie de lui offrir de belles vacances, mais on comprend qu'au fond il est profondément triste et terriblement seul. Il est père célibataire, confronté à des difficultés financières et sans véritable entourage, il porte un mal-être qu'il ne parvient plus à surmonter. La fin révèle également que l'on suivait en réalité les souvenirs de Sophie devenue adulte. Avec le recul, elle comprend enfin les signes qu'elle n'avait pas vus enfant et réalise à quel point son père allait mal avant son décès. Même si je n'ai pas été emballé par le rythme du film, je reconnais que cette conclusion est particulièrement touchante et donne une autre dimension a l’histoire .

texto: This was a nostalgic watch that took me on this melancholic trip to the summer of my own childhood, a summer that would last forever before it's September and it's back to school again, before the 7 am alarm and the traffic jam and the lunch boxes. It's a summer full of long boring afternoons sitting in front of the tv watching whatever comes on. It's the swimming pool days with its fresh juices and short friendships that only last for a day. It's the sand in your hair and your flip-flops, the rosy sun-kissed cheeks, and the extra-defined curls due to the salty water. It's ice cream for breakfast and lunch, it's game nights and cold pizza for dinner, It's throwing off the sheets as the heat pours through your open window through that one long summer night. it's your mother looking young as ever, and your father while he was still doing his best. and your siblings as foolish and stupid as ever. This movie was all that to me, live footage of a life we all lived. I guess that's what makes it so special and hits this deep spot in anyone who watched it, it's how we all had those summers we long for now that we can't escape this adulthood world. My rating reflects my enjoyment of the movie, and in fact I was bored most of the time, I was never fan of those “nothing is really happening” movies.

texto: At its best moments "Aftersun" is a tender and beautiful film about a separated dad spending holidays with his young daughter during the 90s'. For 2/3 of its time, "Aftersun" is filled with charming moments of perfect chemistry between Frankie Corio and Paul Mescal. The problem begins when Charlotte Wells pushes drama into her debut feature, unnaturally brought up, to break the built bonds. The so-called "reflection twenty years later" (from the description) works even less as the only few minutes of the adult Sophie's life do not cover the gap of " the man she didn't" knew.

texto: why can’t we give ourselves one more chance? this isn’t the actual lyric, but i’ve always misinterpreted it as this and it makes more sense to me. a pretty stunning feature debut from wells, somewhere in between after yang and petite maman. oke moves the camera with all the measured physicality of claire denis and is almost yang-reminiscent in his interest in reflections. i love the confidence on display here and indulgence is great, but i do think that at a certain point, there are negative returns from the overuse of oke’s technique. the way hands and arms and interiors are framed is great at showing sophie’s curiosity at the unfamiliar and her burgeoning adolescence/independence, but i don’t think the composite character study is as successful at picking apart calum through her eyes. his empathy radiates in waves, and the inner turmoil is clear, but it’s missing something. god, the climax though. the kid is great and all hail paul mescal.

texto: 54/100 Haven't looked into how autobiographical this is, because that's not important: It feels, in every respect, like the writer-director's bittersweet memories of a vacation she took with her dad at age 11.  Which is to say that it's hyper-specific in detail but largely uneventful, seeking to evoke rather than to dramatize. That's the Terence Davies recipe, but where Davies compresses and magnifies, transforming the mundane into heightened shards of terror and exhilaration and communal spirit, Wells merely remembers (or has an impoverished imagination). Apart from Sophie herself, embodied by Frankie Corio with a thoroughly winning combo of guileless and astringent, nothing registered strongly with me; every filmmaker has this movie in them—we all have childhoods and at least one indelible experience from same—and I appreciate that most choose not to make it, recognizing that what's meaningful to them won't necessarily translate to total strangers. Not without significant formal and/or narrative embellishment, anyway. (Admittedly, Aftersun has many ardent fans, including the NYFF selection committee. But I have a hard time imagining a movie along these lines that they wouldn't love, so long as it's self-evidently heartfelt. Me, I'm enough of a Grinch to demand more.) Wells does ambitiously attempt to suggest an entire contrapuntal narrative, bridging the foregrounded party-like-it-was-1999(-because-it-was) quasi-idyll and a seemingly regretful present, from isolated moments spent with Dad alone, plus very brief glimpses of Sophie as an adult. Intriguing, but it's awfully skeletal, and Paul Mescal, judging from this surface-level performance and his similar work in The Lost Daughter (haven't seen any of Normal People ), just doesn't have the chops to communicate Calum's enigmatic inner torment in a way that would facilitate our understanding of what likely lies in store for the man, and for this relationship. A promising debut, but of the kind that makes you wonder whether there'll be a second film. NOTE: I liked it significantly more the second time .

texto: This was a movie which i didnt understand and definitely need to rewatch. Incredible acting from Mescal and Corio. Was clearly a movie which leans heavily on the bond between father and daughter and deals with the crippling depression which Mescal's character tries to hide from his daughter, Sophie. From the first sort of 20 minutes, you can tell that this film is showing and not telling , whether it's the very long shots focused on a single subject, or the use of solemn and dark composed music for the film within moments which do not warrant it, the film portrays depression in a much more subconscious way than ive seen other films and series manage. The use of the rave scenes, and lingering shots on what seems like random subjects are something I should analyse on a rewatch, as I am no film buff and therefore have not been able to pick up on the purpose of these scenes and what the intention of the cinematography is very well. The consistently sinister or sombre music being draped over the scenes in this film is representative of how depression consumes every waking minute of a person's life. I believe there was also a theme of a young person being introduced to the world of romance and sexual exploration, with lingering shots of teenagers kissing whilst Sophie was nearby, or that one scene of her overhearing some teenagers talking about a sexual experience. I initially assumed that the sinister and sombre music being used during these scenes was to represent how a young individual's introduction to sexual experiences from others educating said person could represent grooming. However upon research for this film's meaning, I found that this might not be the case? Sex as a theme isnt really a topic discussed online (or at least on reddit) So perhaps for that reason I dont think these scenes are about grooming but rather the coming-of-age experience of discovering romance, love and sex as an additional theme ALONGSIDE the depression Sophie's dad suffers from? If it's not clear, I havent fully understood what this movie is actually about. To really get a better understanding of the film I should rewatch it probably. I liked this film a lot, but oh wow I was very confused.

texto: Boah hat der mich eiskalt erwischt. In „Aftersun“ ging ich mit den Erwartungen rein, ein Drama über die Erforschung von Beziehung zwischen Vater und Tochter zu bekommen. Das gab mir der Film auch, aber auch noch so viel härtere Themen. „Aftersun“ fühlte sich für mich wie eine verlorene Erinnerung an meine Kindheit an. Diese Camcorder aufnahmen sind so dermaßen nostalgisch und schön, dass ich alleine da schon hätte heulen können. Das hier ist so toll gefilmt, die Umgebung und das Setting ist herrlich schön anzusehen und die Cinematographie zum dahinschmelzen. Oftmals erinnerte mich „Aftersun“ von der Erzählung und dem Vibe, an „Nowhere“ von Sofia Coppola welchen ich auch echt gerne mochte. Auch dort geht es ja um recht ähnliches, „Aftersun“ macht das aber nochmal ne ganze Stufe besser, meiner Meinung nach. Irgendwo ist „Aftersun“ ein richtiger feelgood-Film, besonders zu Beginn, die Figuren sind im Urlaub und haben einfach Spaß mit der Zeit die sie zusammen verbringen. Gleichzeitig umgibt den gesamten Film eine so bedrückende Atmosphäre und ein Gefühl von Schwere, Anspannung und Nervosität, was ich anfangs etwas seltsam fand, irgendwann aber so grandios für mich funktionierte. Was ich gehört habe, was vielen nicht gefällt, ist das pacing, weil ja, das ist wirklich sehr langsam. Dafür nutzt der Film diese Zeit und Ruhe um die Erzählung richtig aufzubauen und die Figuren uns nahezubringen, was für mich so gut funktioniert hat, wodurch der Film für mich nie langatmig oder gar langweilig war. Ich habe jetzt so viel Positives zu „Aftersun“ gesagt, ohne mein persönliches Highlight des Films zu nennen, Paul Mescal. Paul Mescal spielt wirklich phänomenal gut. Er und Frankie Corio haben erstmal eine 1a Chemie und sind zusammen so dermaßen süß, dazu spielt Paul Mescal diese Figur mit so einer Tiefe, man spürt bei ihm die ganze Zeit, dass er eine Last in sich trägt, welche im Film nie ausgesprochen wird, aber dennoch durch sein Spiel so deutlich ist, das ist unglaublich. „Aftersun“ hat mich mit seiner Thematik und Erzählung unfassbar gepackt, nicht mehr losgelassen und beinahe zu Tränen gerührt. Nur liebe für diesen Film.

texto: !!!! honestly so speechless. this film has my heart. i can't believe this is charlotte's feature debut. many many thoughts that need to be gathered but oh my goodness i loved this so much. so so much. a searing portrait of father-daughter relationships, adolescence, grief, and parenthood set in the 90s told through the process of remembering a holiday in turkey. it feels like a movie that was made for me—may be too early to say but this might be one of my new all time favorites :') laughed cried reflected the whole shabang 1) what a beautiful debut feature by charlotte wells!!! aghh!!! 2) reminded me of somewhere by sofia coppola from 2010, and the lost daughter too 3) gorgeous GORGEOUS cinematography!! so many frames that i'd love to take and just hang on the wall as artwork. gregory oke has such a great great eye 4) the use of mirrors and surface reflections is striking. reminded me of ozu & kogonada—there's one scene where the camera just stays on the reflection of sophie & callum on the TV as they talk about his past and god it was so good 5) the fact that paul mescal is still very much at the beginning of his career and has two films at cannes right now is kinda insane. he was magnificent <3 6) frankie corio is a revelation 🫶🏼 not shutting up about this movie for the rest of the year! the aftersun publicity campaign starts NOW @ espace miramar, 10.15 PM

texto: Aftersun is one of those films that feels incredibly simple on the surface, yet completely devastating underneath. The performances are so natural that they never feel like acting, they feel like real people, which makes the relationship between Sophie and her dad (Callum) deeply personal and relatable. That ordinary, everyday quality is what makes the film so heartbreaking, because it captures the small moments we often overlook until they become memories. Rather than relying on dramatic events, Aftersun quietly builds an emotional weight that lingers long after it ends, leaving a sense of love, loss and regret that feels painfully human.

Was clearly a movie which leans heavily on the bond between father and daughter and deals with the crippling depression which Mescal's character tries to hide from his daughter, Sophie. From the first sort of 20 minutes, you can tell that this film is showing and not telling , whether it's the very long shots focused on a single subject, or the use of solemn and dark composed music for the film within moments which do not warrant it, the film portrays depression in a much more subconscious way than ive seen other films and series manage. The use of the rave scenes, and lingering shots on what seems like random subjects are something I should analyse on a rewatch, as I am no film buff and therefore have not been able to pick up on the purpose of these scenes and what the intention of the cinematography is very well. The consistently sinister or sombre music being draped over the scenes in this film is representative of how depression consumes every waking minute of a person's life. I believe there was also a theme of a young person being introduced to the world of romance and sexual exploration, with lingering shots of teenagers kissing whilst Sophie was nearby, or that one scene of her overhearing some teenagers talking about a sexual experience. I initially assumed that the sinister and sombre music being used during these scenes was to represent how a young individual's introduction to sexual experiences from others educating said person could represent grooming. However upon research for this film's meaning, I found that this might not be the case? Sex as a theme isnt really a topic discussed online (or at least on reddit) So perhaps for that reason I dont think these scenes are about grooming but rather the coming-of-age experience of discovering romance, love and sex as an additional theme ALONGSIDE the depression Sophie's dad suffers from? If it's not clear, I havent fully understood what this movie is actually about. To really get a better understanding of the film I should rewatch it probably. I liked this film a lot, but oh wow I was very confused.

texto: Much like through a foggy lens of a camera, it's a nostalgic reminiscence of that warm and fuzzy summer vacation, blissfully unaware of the realities of adult life, and the anxieties our loved ones can face. Only later on in life do we completely understand how significant these mundane interactions with our loved ones can be, how much meaning our words can have for them, and that we can understand what they once felt. Its emotional core is beautiful. It’s depiction of depression is one of the best I’ve ever seen in a movie, the final shot of Calum walking through the double doors into the night club to symbolize that his life was only ever heading in one direction after the time they spent together is soul crushing. Finally, it’s the lingering memory of a father's love that endures despite the crashing waves of loss and grief

texto: Aftersun is one of those films that feels incredibly simple on the surface, yet completely devastating underneath. The performances are so natural that they never feel like acting, they feel like real people, which makes the relationship between Sophie and her dad (Callum) deeply personal and relatable. That ordinary, everyday quality is what makes the film so heartbreaking, because it captures the small moments we often overlook until they become memories. Rather than relying on dramatic events, Aftersun quietly builds an emotional weight that lingers long after it ends, leaving a sense of love, loss and regret that feels painfully human.

texto: Boah hat der mich eiskalt erwischt. In „Aftersun“ ging ich mit den Erwartungen rein, ein Drama über die Erforschung von Beziehung zwischen Vater und Tochter zu bekommen. Das gab mir der Film auch, aber auch noch so viel härtere Themen. „Aftersun“ fühlte sich für mich wie eine verlorene Erinnerung an meine Kindheit an. Diese Camcorder aufnahmen sind so dermaßen nostalgisch und schön, dass ich alleine da schon hätte heulen können. Das hier ist so toll gefilmt, die Umgebung und das Setting ist herrlich schön anzusehen und die Cinematographie zum dahinschmelzen. Oftmals erinnerte mich „Aftersun“ von der Erzählung und dem Vibe, an „Nowhere“ von Sofia Coppola welchen ich auch echt gerne mochte. Auch dort geht es ja um recht ähnliches, „Aftersun“ macht das aber nochmal ne ganze Stufe besser, meiner Meinung nach. Irgendwo ist „Aftersun“ ein richtiger feelgood-Film, besonders zu Beginn, die Figuren sind im Urlaub und haben einfach Spaß mit der Zeit die sie zusammen verbringen. Gleichzeitig umgibt den gesamten Film eine so bedrückende Atmosphäre und ein Gefühl von Schwere, Anspannung und Nervosität, was ich anfangs etwas seltsam fand, irgendwann aber so grandios für mich funktionierte. Was ich gehört habe, was vielen nicht gefällt, ist das pacing, weil ja, das ist wirklich sehr langsam. Dafür nutzt der Film diese Zeit und Ruhe um die Erzählung richtig aufzubauen und die Figuren uns nahezubringen, was für mich so gut funktioniert hat, wodurch der Film für mich nie langatmig oder gar langweilig war. Ich habe jetzt so viel Positives zu „Aftersun“ gesagt, ohne mein persönliches Highlight des Films zu nennen, Paul Mescal. Paul Mescal spielt wirklich phänomenal gut. Er und Frankie Corio haben erstmal eine 1a Chemie und sind zusammen so dermaßen süß, dazu spielt Paul Mescal diese Figur mit so einer Tiefe, man spürt bei ihm die ganze Zeit, dass er eine Last in sich trägt, welche im Film nie ausgesprochen wird, aber dennoch durch sein Spiel so deutlich ist, das ist unglaublich. „Aftersun“ hat mich mit seiner Thematik und Erzählung unfassbar gepackt, nicht mehr losgelassen und beinahe zu Tränen gerührt. Nur liebe für diesen Film.

texto: Nothing but heartbreaking and heartwarming to recognize that our parents, more specific, our fathers, have their own history before, during and after us, they’re are living for the first time, they’re learning how to raise an small human, they are afraid, they do mistakes, they hide their struggles so we don’t have to worry, they’re strong, they’re weak. We often judge them because they don’t do what we think will be the right thing to do, and we fight, we claim and we get mad. But we forgot their battles and how much they try, and how much they have given us, with all the mistakes they could have made. Sadly maybe we could never understand what they’re going through fully but show unconditional support anytime is the best we can do. I honor the father I have and I hope he knows everyday how proud, how grateful and how much I love him.

texto: c’est un film très lent, avec une atmosphère étrange et de très très très très longs dialogues. c’est un infini procès, avec une embrouille interminable, qui révèle une ambiance très sombre et des personnages tous plus bizarres les uns que les autres. on comprend pas tout et c’est très compliqué d’accrocher. certains plans sont filmées de façon original, et les scènes sont vraiment longues. c’est un film chargé en émotion, avec beaucoup de secrets enfouies. au bout d’un moment ça devient vraiment interminable, des faits surgissent, des hypothèses sont conjecturées, mais c’est jamais explicitement concret. bon ok la façon dont c’est réalisé est très intéressante. par contre, j’ai carrément détesté la fin, pcq tout le long on s’attend à une réponse concrète mais le but du film c’est justement de ne donner aucune réponse, du coup c’est super frustrant. toute l’histoire on peut l’interpréter seulement par des « peut être » et jamais par de véritables faits. chacun des personnages sont intéressants, avec des points de vus différents et des façons de subir la situation différentes, mais le spectateur est à la place des jurés, donc c’est très compliqué de savoir démêlé le vrai du faux. le film rappelle que le verdict ne coïncide pas forcément avec la vérité, et les hypothèses de la potentielle vérité restent plausible. cependant le lien avec le titre du film est très pertinent, en montrant la chute de chacun des personnages de façon disséquées. bon, en toute honnêteté je n’ai pas aimé. le fond du film est émouvant et bien recherché. MAIS, c’est lent + dialogues interminables + bcp de choses abstraites et surtout surtout surtout le film répond à rien, ça te laisse sur ta fin, c’est à toi d’interpréter et de trouver la vérité, la fin est ouverte et ne répond à aucune questions que tu te poses durant tout le film. c’est frustrant et c’est carrément ce que je n’aime pas.

texto: Palme d’or 2023 et couronné de nombreuses récompenses, Anatomie d’une chute de Justine Triet mérite largement sa réputation. Derrière son apparence de film judiciaire se cache avant tout une dissection fascinante d’un couple en crise, où chaque détail du quotidien prend une importance capitale. Le suspense autour de ce whodunit atypique fonctionne parfaitement, mais le véritable sujet est ailleurs : les ressentis, les incompréhensions et les visions opposées que deux personnes peuvent avoir d’une même histoire. Sandra Hüller livre une prestation remarquable, parvenant à transmettre une multitude d’émotions d’un simple regard. Une réalisation subtile qui nous plonge au plus près des émotions des personnages. Un très bon film.

texto: This was awesome. Might be a higher score on rewatch. I’m gonna sleep and give my full thoughts tomorrow. Best Criterion purchase I made since Memories of Murder . ________________________________________________________ Anatomy of a Fall enticed me from the premise alone. A woman is blamed for her husband’s death and the only witness is her blind son. That in it of itself is enough to get my attention. The film is an amazing courtroom drama. It’s similar to A Few Good Men in that every single court sequence is riveting, filled with incredible dialogue and tense confrontations. The movie does a great job creating suspense and tension. I genuinely did not know how it was all gonna play out. What makes this movie stand out though is at its heart, it’s a family drama. It’s about a marriage on the brink of collapse, and how the couple’s issues are impacting their loved ones. It tackles very real topics like infidelity, sexuality, childhood, abuse, depression, and grief. I found myself caring about these characters and the struggles they endured throughout the movie’s runtime. Everything about this movie felt real. Never once did I feel like I was watching a movie. Anatomy of a Fall felt more like someone hid a camera inside someone’s house rather than actors reciting lines from a script (a very well written script I might add) in front of a camera. The authenticity of this film is thanks equally to the screen writer(s) and the actors. Sandra Hüller in particular is downright incredible. The realism of this movie is a bit of a blessing and a curse. I love that the director allowed certain scenes to “breathe.” It created a bunch of heartfelt moments and it gives the viewer the chance to sit with these characters and empathize with them. That being said, I felt like some scenes dragged on for a little too long, and it ruined the pacing in some parts. But once again, maybe on second watch, I’ll feel differently. Bottom line, I love Anatomy of a Fall . I can’t wait to watch it again. In fact I kinda have to watch it again. I watched it while my wife was at book club. When she returned and realized I was watching this movie, she was like “OMG I wanted to watch that too!” Sorry babe. 😜

texto: Mettez du respect et de la lumière sur le cinéma féminin. Un film de procès qui ne cherche jamais vraiment le verdict, mais la faille. Triet construit son récit comme une dissection minutieuse du couple, où chaque certitude s'effrite à mesure que le tribunal (et le spectateur) croit avancer. Sandra Hüller y est habitée d'une opacité fascinante : on ne sait jamais si son intelligence est une armure ou un aveu. Mais au-delà du dispositif judiciaire, c'est une question bien plus vertigineuse que pose le film : connaît-on vraiment l'autre ? Son voisin, son frère, sa sœur, son ou sa compagne ? Aucune famille n'échappe aux secrets de polichinelle, à ces zones d'ombre qui persistent sans jamais être nommées. Chaque foyer a ses casseroles, ses non-dits tolérés en silence. C'est ce qui rend le film aussi dramatique que profondément humain. Il ne s'agit pas de juger un couple, mais de mesurer combien la connaissance intime de l'autre [ et de soi-même ] reste toujours partielle, négociée, parfois illusoire. Une leçon d'humilité face à la complexité des êtres. La mise en scène, souvent austère, presque clinique, épouse cette froideur alpine du chalet, comme si le décor lui-même refusait de trancher. C'est là toute l'ambiguïté du film : il ne raconte pas une mort mais l'impossibilité de connaître véritablement l'autre même après des années de vie commune. Les 2h30 pèsent par moments, notamment dans les longueurs procédurales qui, même si elles nourrissent le vertige du doute, testent aussi la patience. L'usage de l'anglais, pivot thématique plus que coquetterie, dérange certains. J'avoue que j'ai eu du mal avec ce yoyo entre les langues mais c'est à tort selon moi, tant il matérialise la distance entre les langues, les cultures, et finalement entre les personnes elles-mêmes. texto: This was awesome. Might be a higher score on rewatch. I’m gonna sleep and give my full thoughts tomorrow. Best Criterion purchase I made since Memories of Murder . ________________________________________________________ Anatomy of a Fall enticed me from the premise alone. A woman is blamed for her husband’s death and the only witness is her blind son. That in it of itself is enough to get my attention. The film is an amazing courtroom drama. It’s similar to A Few Good Men in that every single court sequence is riveting, filled with incredible dialogue and tense confrontations. The movie does a great job creating suspense and tension. I genuinely did not know how it was all gonna play out. What makes this movie stand out though is at its heart, it’s a family drama. It’s about a marriage on the brink of collapse, and how the couple’s issues are impacting their loved ones. It tackles very real topics like infidelity, sexuality, childhood, abuse, depression, and grief. I found myself caring about these characters and the struggles they endured throughout the movie’s runtime. Everything about this movie felt real. Never once did I feel like I was watching a movie. Anatomy of a Fall felt more like someone hid a camera inside someone’s house rather than actors reciting lines from a script (a very well written script I might add) in front of a camera. The authenticity of this film is thanks equally to the screen writer(s) and the actors. Sandra Hüller in particular is downright incredible. The realism of this movie is a bit of a blessing and a curse. I love that the director allowed certain scenes to “breathe.” It created a bunch of heartfelt moments and it gives the viewer the chance to sit with these characters and empathize with them. That being said, I felt like some scenes dragged on for a little too long, and it ruined the pacing in some parts. But once again, maybe on second watch, I’ll feel differently. Bottom line, I love Anatomy of a Fall . I can’t wait to watch it again. In fact I kinda have to watch it again. I watched it while my wife was at book club. When she returned and realized I was watching this movie, she was like “OMG I wanted to watch that too!” Sorry babe. 😜

texto: Palme d’or 2023 et couronné de nombreuses récompenses, Anatomie d’une chute de Justine Triet mérite largement sa réputation. Derrière son apparence de film judiciaire se cache avant tout une dissection fascinante d’un couple en crise, où chaque détail du quotidien prend une importance capitale. Le suspense autour de ce whodunit atypique fonctionne parfaitement, mais le véritable sujet est ailleurs : les ressentis, les incompréhensions et les visions opposées que deux personnes peuvent avoir d’une même histoire. Sandra Hüller livre une prestation remarquable, parvenant à transmettre une multitude d’émotions d’un simple regard. Une réalisation subtile qui nous plonge au plus près des émotions des personnages. Un très bon film.

texto: Great score, Jimmy’s pretty decent but not by courtroom drama standards. I can’t for the life of me understand the rave reviews?! Hokey acting, stilted/unnatural framing, rather quaint manners and niceties that don’t age well, way too long a runtime for its sleepy pacing and not that interesting a crime, anyway. I won’t even mention the glossing over a rape in so many instances, because that’s unfortunately how the justice system works, even now. Nowhere near the level of Witness For The Prosecution, 12 Angry Men, To Kill A Mockingbird, never mind more recent, relevant movies that haven’t dated terribly.

texto: A long, boring, simplistic, contrived, and nonsensical imitation of Witness for the Prosecution [1957] , with a misleading title, irrelevant opening credit animation, and silly ending soliloquy all probably intended to remind you of the plot of 12 Angry Men [1957] , that tries too hard to be "edgy", while wasting its runtime not trying hard enough to understand what made its predecessors work. The only good thing about Anatomy of a Murder [1959] is its jazz score. Co-watcher: "I felt like I was on jury duty, and wasn't getting paid for it."

texto: I wish I could excuse problematic aspects since it's a film made in the 1950s if it was at least somewhat engaging. Close to nothing worked for me. Jimmy Stewart is one of my favorite actors but this is his least memorable role from those that I've seen. A movie that revolves around rape and murder tries to be empathetic to the victim and crtique too rigid "appropriate" dress standards for women but then revolves a lot of the trial and evidence around it anyway and the ending ends up turning a blind eye to a husband beating his wife. It also feels tone deaf to have so many comedic moments despite the subject matter and it generally feels like the filmmakers never treat the case seriously enough, which is weird since it is is based on a true story. It's dull, repetitive and emotionally hollow with one dimensional characters. A waste of time.

texto: At its best, Anatomy of a Murder is a compelling courtroom drama that showcases the flawless ability of James Stewart and touches on some rather radical takes on understanding why rape culture is so often dismissed and ignored in the court of law. However, the film gets so deep in the repetitive proceedings of the court that it stretches to an absurd 160-minute runtime. Things grow SLOW, and the energy seen in films like 12 Angry Men and The Caine Mutiny Court-Martial fades more and more as the runtime drags. There is the occasional shocking reveal or particularly venomous twist of facts, but for the most part this feels like it is lacking a needed intensity for choosing a scope of this size.

texto: It's a strange film... ​At first glance, the filmmakers seem to think that the heart of the matter lies in whether the wife of the murderer has been violated or not—except they don't. Justifiably so, as they themselves declare in the movie, since that would still not make the murder permissible. Then they swerve to an after-the-fact plea of temporary insanity on the thinnest of evidence. ​The attorney (Stewart) raises smokescreen after smokescreen regarding the possible rape and the murder victim's character, offering very little to substantiate their central defense claim. This, too, his very character admits. I understand exactly what the film is doing here: it is a deliberate critique of the US legal system and juries, exposing the courtroom as a cynical game where truth takes a backseat to theatrics. ​However, while I get the point, the execution feels far too clinical. Spending nearly three hours meticulously building a courtroom drama only to conclude that the entire system is fundamentally broken—and that the truth doesn't actually matter—almost invalidates the film's own narrative. If the whole process is just an empty sham, watching it play out for that long ultimately becomes uninteresting. Because of this detachment, all the characters remain mere caricatures that we never examine more than skin deep. While the filmmakers likely intended to provoke these exact moral questions, the execution is so dry that it feels like reading a well-argued college essay—intellectually sound, perhaps, but it doesn't make for an engaging film. It's a strange film...

texto: fun watch insofar as a trial lawyer, i find trial fun - and some legitimately good trial strategy in here (aided by the fact that in a movie courtroom you get to wax poetic about your objections in the presence of the jury) but nothing profound; difficult not to compare to witness for the prosecution, which i just also watched and liked a bit more; though ultimately i am glad they both deal with, in some way, the idea that our justice system tolerates, as it should, the non-conviction of people who did bad things i genuinely may use this banger quote in a closing: "Twelve people go off into a room: twelve different minds, twelve different hearts, from twelve different walks of life; twelve sets of eyes, ears, shapes, and sizes. And these twelve people are asked to judge another human being as different from them as they are from each other. And in their judgment, they must become of one mind - unanimous. It's one of the miracles of Man's disorganized soul that they can do it, and in most instances, do it right well. God bless juries."

exemplo: Algumas reviews criticam a forma como o filme aborda a violência sexual e o sexismo, considerando que há momentos problemáticos e que a obra reflete atitudes datadas.
texto: This movie is obviously sexist and dated. It could not and should not be made today with its understanding of rape and women’s autonomy. At the same time, the legal aspect of the story is the most interesting, where the characters have to justify themselves in a court of law, where their fates are determined by their ability to perform in the legal circus. The film is true to its time and enshrines many of the ideals of the 1950s while acknowledging that the world was changing (discussions of sex and sexual assault spoken about plainly—if uncomfortably—in defiance of the Hays code). The best part is hands down Duke Ellington’s score.

texto: I think i respect this film more than i actually enjoyed it, though i still did the latter. It must have been shockingly frank and transgressive against 1949's modest culture- anyone who's seen a black-and-white movie before could tell you this wasn't normal. Maybe that's why the era's exaggerated acting style distracted me more than it normally does- it's an impressively modern film, but today those modernisms serve to draw a greater contrast against its anachronisms. Still, it's a deeply nuanced and open-ended story. Never am I told how to feel about these people, never do they explain their sense of morality to the camera- I'm left on my own to feel out my own sense of right and wrong in this fictional case, and through it, the legal system at large.

texto: This movie was... Okay. It was hard getting into at first with a slow exposition, not to mention how long this movie is. Because of when it was made there are some moments that are just blatantly sexist and racist. Though, once it gets to the main action (the court room scenes, not that exciting i suppose) it starts to get better. The plot twist near the end of the movie was unexpected, but I could see the foreshadowing for it. Overall, it was a pretty average film, nothing stands out to me too much. I recommend this movie if you like watching investigations, enjoy a slower paced plot, and are fine with seeing a black and white film.

texto: It's been quite a few years since I've watched this one and it didn't really live up to the memories on repeat watch.  It's got all the ingredients you'd want from the central Jimmy Stewart performance, the Saul Bass designs and a Duke Ellington Score, sadly it doesn't really have the script to go with it.  I'm sure this was a pretty daring subject matter for the time it was made but the actual court case itself is never really that compelling or does it ever carry sufficient enough intrigue.  The runtime is honestly ludicrous, and even though you're always invested throughout it, it's never really at any point completely justified.

texto: A courtroom drama that paints the law in a plain, morally gray light. Actually feels like you’re in the courtroom just watching a trial, albeit with some outbursts that feel like they wouldn't fly in real life. With this movie being so morally gray, I found it hard to find someone to root for. I believe that’s the point, but it’s a confusing feeling and not one I enjoyed here. I also did not enjoy the ending. Talk about anticlimactic. They adjourn for the day and then they come back and read the verdict and that’s it, movie over. There was no “silver-bullet” moment in which I was convinced that jury was going to vote one way or the other. So I was still ultimately unconvinced and I personally find it hard to believe the jury was convinced as well. Definitely knocked this movie down a peg for me. While a bit slow, I found the case and performances compelling. The jazz score was nice as well, when you could actually hear it. The court scenes had no score at all. Envelope-pushing and edgy for the time, but I don’t understand the adoration for this movie.

texto: Anatomy of a Murder forms quite an intriguing investigative drama. This confidently serves up what is perhaps the most comprehensive onscreen treatment of the judicial process. Frank matter-of-fact discussion of the main subject matter must've been quite the shock back in the "squeaky-clean" times of 1959. The counselors don't beat around the bush here. They talk about sex, rape, and murder... for lack of better terms. It's striking how relevant that particular aspect rings nowadays, especially in regard to how lawyers, officers, and judicial figures speak about women in cases involving them in any capacity. While inspired by an actual case circa 1952, the film feels ahead of its time in laying out the information to the audience. Otto Preminger's patient, level-headed direction allows what could've been melodrama to instead become a true-to-life mystery... and a fascinating mental exercise. James Stewart reliably offers yet another excellent performance. It's clever how this film plays with the trusted authority type we'd expect him to fill, notably when the trial gets heated. The ensemble cast acquits themselves superbly (no pun intended). Lee Remmick treads the line between desperate wife and seductive femme like the palm of her hand. Ben Gazzarra spiritedly lends intensity and grit into his defendant, fueling the stakes in his position. George C. Scott, Orson Bean, and Joseph N. Welch steal their scenes with such vivid presence (loud or quiet). The strength of all their performances on top of an astute script already warrants a physical media purchase. Preminger takes it further by developing an absorbing style that enables the back-and-forth to be so engaging. Charm, warmth, intrigue, and crackling dialogue foster strong interest well before the defense accepts their client. I would advise against watching this late at night, lest you become sleepy and miss a crucial moment. texto: This movie was not exactly what I was expecting. I feel as though it could more accurately have been called Anatomy of a Rape with its surprisingly prominent repeated references to panties and an explanation of spermatogenesis , which I was definitely not expecting in a movie from 1959. Right up to the end I was anticipating there to be a twist, and of course there was, although I have to say that it was something of a letdown. Nevertheless there were some wonderful lines of dialogue in the snappy exchanges between the lawyers and the judge and some unexpectedly humourous moments. However it is a really long movie which undoubtedly drags a bit on occasions with its very lengthy courtroom scenes. There was undeniably inappropriate sexual tension between Jimmy Stewart as the defendant's lawyer and Lee Remick as the defendant's wife, as she confidently stated in a matter-of-fact way, that, of course he was gazing upon her lustfully, as all men do. Also some typically sixties sexism in Pauly’s interactions with his assistant Maida, who for me was still the best character. In the end I managed to forgive any such shortcomings as incidental, putting them down to being merely a consequence of the era, and enjoyed the complexities of the movie immensely. Sue me. Oh yes, bonus points for Muffy the dog.

texto: The way how well a narrative is laid out before the jury determines all. I doubted the story as a watcher but if I was in that court room only, I’d have believed Paulie. It’s funny how things are told to cut out from the record but what really matters is that the jury heard what was said. Paulie knows it so well. The prosecutor was fumbling hard without everyone else on his team. Watching the whole case unfold, it just made me go justice isn’t really real. It’s ruled by narrative more than just hard evidence. It’s a bleak look. Even the judge got charmed by Paulie and his fishing hobby talk. Paulie genuinely didn’t wanna take this case and I kinda get him. It’s so much trouble especially when it’s clear that there’s a reason why the lieutenant is locked up. I super hated the questioning scene of the rape and details from Laura. It felt so humiliating. All routes of questioning lead to misogyny. It doesn’t even matter if the rape happened or not cause they already sentence her character from the way she dresses and interacts with the world. It’s the same case for Mary whose character is questioned so much that she’s forced to reveal her relationship.  There’s nothing much crazy happening in this movie but the dialogue exchange is so fast paced and keeps everything moving. Pauline’s friendship with his recovering alcoholic friend and his secretary is cute. Their next case being helping Mary out is messed up but I guess that’s a lawyer’s integrity.

texto: A vapid, underwhelming and utterly predictable "thriller". It's such a slog, which is specially offensive considering it's 2,5 hours long runtime, and, at the end of it all, there was hardly something worth building up to. It tries to be artsy with its quiet contemplative moments and its purposeful vagueness, it tries to be political with its commentary and """world-building""", but doesn't really nail any of it. The characters are implied to be full of depth and trauma, but none of it is developed, nor has any point in the end. Just a pointless 2,5 hours, that were only slightly salvaged by Steven Yeun's wonderful performance.

texto: I really wasn’t the biggest fan of this movie even though I really wanted to be. Nothing really ever clicked for me to like this, I really disliked how open ended they kept it. I’m usually a fan of keeping something ambiguous but just feel like their attempt at it fell flat. The first 30 minutes were basically pointless, just showed a sex scene and two scenes just watching the main character jerk off. It really doesn’t start to get going until Steven Yeuns character pulls up. Even when he comes in it still feels extremely slow and avoids really digging deep into any big ideas. Really didn’t feel any suspense towards the end when it tries to turn into a thriller type of vibe. The main charter was so unlikeable, at his core he was a total loser who takes all his built up anger out on Ben in a pretty messy climax to the movie. I did really enjoy the cinematography and Steven Yeuns performance. Besides that I was not a fan, it also really didn’t help that the subtitles were about 2 seconds ahead of the dialogue so it was very hard to follow a lot of the dialogue. May need a rewatch because of this.

texto: In the Burning, Jong-su the main character wants to become a writer, but he almost never writes, his life seems to have a certain emptiness, And he doesn’t seem to really pay much attention or take much agency for most of the movie. Jong su meets a girl he knew from his childhood, Hae mi, and they start spending time together until she leaves for a trip to Africa, and she asks him to watch her cat while she is away. When she returns, she isn’t alone but with a new mysterious friend named Ben. He is apparently wealthy, and his life appears much more put together, a stark contrast compared to Jong Su. After spending some time together with Ben and Hae mi, one evening, Ben reveals his odd hobby to Jong Su. After the reveal of Ben's hobby, the movie starts feeling very sinister and at times eerie. And this reveal sets off a chain of events that consume Jong Su but also for the first time give him a certain meaning, and he starts taking some action but in the process also confusing both Jong Su but also us, the viewers, and with no real explanation to any of them, the movie remains purposefully vague, and it keeps us guessing as to what has really happened and hasn’t happened, keeping the burning truth obscured by smoke. The character of Hae mi plays an important role in translating the message of the movie, and how the characters interact with her might be one of the most important parts of the whole movie. We know from certain characters that her life is a mess, but she doesn’t really let us see this, or maybe Jong-su at first just wasn’t looking hard enough (just like the viewer being focused on the mystery), not really caring about her but mostly seeing her and her body as an object. Jong-su appears helpless to the competition from Ben, while maybe also feeling resentment towards him because of their class differences. Hae mi is concerned with her life’s meaning and purpose. Ben and Jong-su are more concerned over who will have “ownership” over her. 4/5

texto: Very subtle and creeping directorial style, really it's almost unnoticeable with how naturally the story flows from start to finish. You really have to pay close attention to fully appreciate its brilliance. The film's use of natural light was awesome, the cinematography had this way of making even the most unremarkable locations aesthetically pleasing. I love how the narrative took its time establishing and really building up the characters, as it progresses, further depth is added to each of them, which kept the mystery really gripping and unpredictable. I thought the film chose the best and most satisfying path to conclude on, answering the question regarding her whereabouts would've been lame, especially after all that amazing buildup. I usually dislike these type of ending because they often feel more like the director just wasn't able to provide a satisfactory answer to the question they posed, but in this film's case it's different, it didn't feel like a cop out, but really more of a conscious choice, one that encourages a further and more in depth rewatch.

tema: Crítica social e desigualdade de classe
exemplo: O filme é visto como uma crítica contundente às disparidades de classe na Coreia do Sul, explorando a tensão entre um protagonista de origem humilde e um personagem rico e misterioso, com comentários sobre privilégio e alienação.
texto: What strikes me the most about Lee Chang-dong's Burning is that throughout its entire 2 hour and 28 minute runtime, nothing happens. This is partly untrue, Burning's second half concedes to some minute thriller conventions but never fully yields to being a standard, by the book thriller. Instead, much of it is this masculine ego war between two men. Two men from completely opposite social classes. The first of these two men is Jong-su, an aspiring writer unable to find employment in Korea's rigidly competitive job market. He's curious and always questions the world around him, and he's very well aware of his class standing. He's aware of the material conditions around him, and he seems to have some sort of knowledge on the issues of capitalism and imperialism (even if this is never outwardly revealed). And standing opposing to him is Ben. Ben is this mysterious figure who stands blissfully ignorant to the world around him. He gets to do so because he's one of the upper elites. And when the inciting incident about halfway into the film occurs, the film becomes a silent battle between the two, attempting to dominate the other, Jong-su channeling his jealousy of Ben's lifestyle while Ben attempts to use his status to elevate himself over Jong-su. However, it is almost impossible to talk about Burning without mentioning the most important character of the film (in my opinion at least), is Hae-Mi. If Jong-su represented the alienation and repressed anger of the lower class Koreans, Hae-Mi serves as an allegory for how women are stripped of their agency under capitalism and its brutal class system. Early on the film, Hae-Mi is introduced to the audience as an old friend of Jong-su, and they go for a dinner together. Here she explains two metaphors, "Little Hunger" and "Great Hunger". "Little Hunger", she says, is the immediate desires of humanity, to fulfill their literal hunger and to survive. However, she then elaborates that the "Great Hunger" is humanity's hunger for meaning in life, some objective truth to the absurdity we live in. Her story is one of the most important parts of the film, yet it is completely depicted through the eyes of Jong-su. It is established that he is completely obsessed over her, yet the film never highlights how much of that love is truly real, or is some infatuation. Through his gaze, she is completely stripped of her agency, mirroring the film's commentary on patriarchy in a Korean society as well. When Hae-Mi dances in the sunset, high on weed and naked from the top, the film drifts into its most hypnotic and stunning. The visuals are truly incredible during this scene, and I was utterly captivated throughout her ritualistic performance. Jong-sus jealousy of her and Ben turned into misogyny and here, as he angrily refers to her as a "whore", the audience begins to see the pent up anger spew out with uncomfortable misogyny, which boils into the final act of the film. Yet, as the end arrived, the film refused to provide any answers. Which is why the ending had more than a few people feel it was futile. There's no final answer, no twist to shock the viewers. Nothing. With this, Lee Chang-dong even questions the genre's conventions of objective finalities, that the final act of violence has any meaning in solving the mystery of the film. The film asserts the mystery isn't the point, the pointlessness IS the point. Whether an objective truth can ever be found is unlikely, all humanity can live on are interpretations of narratives and ideas we build in our heads.

exemplo: O filme é visto como uma crítica contundente às disparidades de classe na Coreia do Sul, explorando a tensão entre um protagonista de origem humilde e um personagem rico e misterioso, com comentários sobre privilégio e alienação.
texto: I have less to say about Burning than I thought I would. Perhaps I found it too slow or cold. I wanted it to grab me with emotion or mystery or provocation, but for the most part, Burning just simmers. Of course, I think this is the point. I suppose there’s any number of themes available for examination, but I interpreted Burning to be a study in main character syndrome. Lee Jong-su is more or less idled in life. By some combination of his social class and passivity, he is unable to find his footing. So, when Hae-mi (re)enters his frame, and subsequently offers a portal into a life of privilege and agency vis-à-vis Ben, Jong-su spirals. There’s too much ambiguity over the course of the movie for it to be unintentional; yet we watch as Jong-su haphazardly rushes to solve, villainize, and intervene. But it’s too late. In time, it becomes clear that he is leaping to conclusions because the potential for his life to finally develop some meaning is too intoxicating. These ideas are potent, even emotional. For that reason alone, I can recommend Burning with ease. I wish I had loved it, but I’m glad I at least found it great.

texto: cerita perlawanan kelas pekerja terhadap orang kaya yang semena-mena itu selalu berhasil membeli (tidak dalam ruang kapitalisme) saya. belum lagi kini protagonisnya beresonansi dengan saya pribadi yang sama-sama penulis novel yang belum juga debut (bedanya naskah saya sudah diterima dan dalam tahap pengeditan) yang membuat film ini terasa begitu dekat dengan saya pribadi. sebelum masuk ke filmnya sendiri, perlu diketahui saya adalah pembaca sastra jepang yang tidak terlalu suka Haruki Murakami. di novelnya yang berjudul Norwegian Wood, saya sampai harus mencorat-coret satu halaman saking terganggunya dengan adegan seksual yang sebegitu eksplisitnya. bukannya saya anti dengan penggambaran seks dalam konteks sastra, akan tetapi menggambarkannya dengan mentah dan hanya berfokus pada “tata cara mengeluarkan sperma dalam dua halaman” bukanlah sesuatu yang menarik di mata saya. seks seharusnya dapat digambarkan dengan indah dan penuh dinamika kuasa. bisa kok adegan seks itu ditulis dalam rangka menunjukan seberapa telanjang seseorang di hadapan masalah yang ia hadapi atau seberapa kuat seseorang memegang peranan orang lainnya dalam menggerakan cerita. apapun itu, ini dapat diolah menjadi sesuatu yang punya nilai tambah dalam ceritanya itu sendiri. tetapi ya mungkin kebanyakan pembaca suka-suka saja dengan sajian yang seperti ini. di film ini saya tidak menemukan itu. Hae-mi berhasil dibuat sebagai gadis yang menggerakan Jongsu di adegan seks mereka. ada dinamika kuasa yang ditaruh di sana. ditambah bayangan di dinding selagai mereka melakukan itu juga yang memberikan petunjuk tambahan di filmnya sendiri. jadi adegannya tidak serta merta jadi penambah keseksian storytelling Lee Chang-dong. cerita dijalani dengan lamban tetapi tidak membosankan karena selalu ada yang terjadi. kamera dibuat seperti pena yang meliuk, menebar prosa di mana-mana. beberapa dibiarkan tanpa dialog. beberapa kali juga tanpa suara. seru sekali, seperti melihat seorang penyair sedang berpuisi dengan intonasi serta penekanan yang pas. iya, betul. yang pas. bukan yang seperti lomba puisi tingkat kabupaten yang semua pesertanya memakai intonasi yang sama padahal puisinya berkonsep jenaka. kita disuguhkan karakter bernama Ben, seorang kaya yang nggak jelas pekerjaannya apa. kurang lebih seperti orang-orang yang kita sering lihat di pagi hari sedang joging santai dengan kacamata hitam dan earphone di telinganya, ketika kita sendiri sedang berdesak-desakan di dalam transjakarta dengan para pekerja (dan pencari kerja) lainnya. kadang saya berpikir, “mereka kerjanya apa ya?” dan pertanyaan itulah yang ditanyakan Jongsu di awal pertemuan mereka. Haemi di sini ditempatkan sebagai hiburan untuk Ben dan teman-temannya (yang saya yakin bermasalah juga). Sama seperti yang terjadi dewasa ini, di mana kalangan menengah ke bawah disawer di platform digital selama mereka menari-nari tidak jelas di depan kamera ponselnya yang berkabut. di luar tampak seperti berkarya tetapi sejatinya kita memang hanyalah boneka hiburan kala mereka bosan saja. di sinilah yang memberakan Jongsu dengan Haemi. Jongsu menyadari itu. mereka tidak pernah benar-benar peduli dengan kita, mereka cuma melihat kita lucu. seperti anak-anak kampung yang melepas sendal saat masuk mall (saya sendiri hehe) dan ditertawakan oleh anak komplek. Haemi sama seperti itu, sedangkan Jongsu tidak. kenapa? karena dia terjamah pendidikan. pernah ada ungkapan dari seorang rusia yang hobi berceloteh, “penderitaan adalah untuk mereka yang intelek nan penuh empati.”. intelektualitas dibangun dari pendidikan. tidak melulu pendidikan formal kok. Jongsu diperlihatkan sebagai seorang yang gemar membaca (uniknya tanpa ada adegan dia membaca). rumahnya dipenuhi buku-buku yang berserakan, tipikal karakter lelaki yang ditulis Haruki Murakami. ini yang membuat kepekaannya lebih tajam melihat kondisi sosial mereka. hanya saja seorang intelek tidaklah mampu berbuat apa-apa ketika di hadapannya adalah seorang raja jahat yang memiliki segalanya. bagi saya, di akhir film, dan hanya di akhir film, film ini menjadi metafiksi. adegan terakhir adalah bagaimana kita bisa terus berkhayal (untuk suatu hari kejadian) bahwa kita juga punya kuasa di hadapan mereka. seperti Jongsu yang menulis ceritanya sendiri, kita juga suatu saat dapat membalikan keadaan di mana kita tidak lagi ditindas oleh mereka. tentu jika dan hanya jika kita semua bersatu, bukan seperti saat ini, yang kota saling meninju, membiarkan para kaya raya itu berlari pagi dengan hati dan hari yang penuh ketenangan, mengetahui mereka tidak perlu tersentuh apa-apa. eat the (bad) rich, soon.

texto: Idk. Sometime around Inglorious Basterds Tarantino crawled way too far up his own ass and he started trying to elevate his style of airy pulpy pastiche by grounding it in these very historicized settings and trying his hand at some revisionism. I think this largely exposes his strengths and weaknesses as a filmmaker, his strengths being that he knows a lot about movies and is inspired by some of the best filmmakers and films of new Hollywood and his earnest efforts of carrying that tradition on is touching, and his weaknesses being that he’s stupid and has very close minded views of everything and has very reactionary sensibilities. Hard to muster much of my thoughts on Django specifically because all of QTs films follow the same beats and thus have the same structural flaws. But I’ll say that while there’s a lot of righteous violence and catharsis for Django against white slavers, there is equal parts gratuitous violence against black slaves used for little more than exploitative window dressing.

texto: i feel like i’m crazy. this movie is so indulgent, so exploitative, and so gratuitous. i think it’s a necessary story. pre-civil war and the arc of a freed black man as a western makes a lot of sense. tarantino was not the man who should have done it, and the tone of this film is insulting. this setting is not the one for dark comedy. people can do what they want, they can enjoy what they want, but i find this film completely irresponsible. not only do we still have a white savior in mr. schultz, but we spend the most time with a black slave owner as an antagonist. the film plays white antagonism as a joke or comedic relief, while samuel l. jackson is played like a real villain. i suppose there is an argument to be made for dicaprio, but mr. shultz defeats him, not even our black protagonist. the messaging is all over the place. it fails to comment on the lack of true power black people could ever have in this time period by being dishonest about the positions of power they are put in in this film. the other enslaved people we see, other than the people being whipped or eaten by dogs, seem peaceful and willing. i think it paints an inaccurate picture. not to mention, what good does it do to show so much violence against enslaved people? we can use it sparingly, that’s okay, but general audiences won’t understand the gravity of the violence against enslaved people when they see it within a comedy like this. “American Slavery Was Not A Sergio Leone Spaghetti Western. It Was A Holocaust. My Ancestors Are Slaves. Stolen From Africa. I Will Honor Them.“ - spike lee maybe i’m missing something. please enlighten me. but i found this to be egregious.

texto: took me awhile to pinpoint why this film bothered me so much, then just now i realized its like those videos of men hunting down and pummeling  pedos in parking lots,  finding a socially acceptable target to release pent up passions against humanity, the love story doesnt work either cause that would take tarantino to know what love is. is he criticizing what slave owners did to black women or is he , again, finding a socially acceptable "historically accurate" excuse to portray women how he likes them? there actually seemed to be very little sympathy for enslaved people, and primarily just hatred for the enslavers , and youd never defend a slave owner getting his brains blown out, right? and yet this film almost made me feel like a pacifist nonviolent liberal, i could look past a lot of the almost "fascist liberalism" (idk what else to call it, proggresive films that feel fascist due to story structure + tone +++ misogyny ) and still enjoy inglorious basterds cause i honestly just love the technical mastery of that film (also its so funny ToT), tarantino copies the good stuff and the film looks  brilliant, its hard to believe it was made by the same guy  as this, some scenes have brilliant values, composition, camerawork too, but so much of the film is so mediocre on a technical scale, some shots felt so lazy and common, like he settled on the first boring idea that came to his head also so funny that waltz of all people won an oscar, im so sorry, i say this with love, but he plays the same character in everything he does - even interviews! like thats just him!!! ,same mannerisms, same everything hes just playing himself,  hans landa made more sense since up until that point he refused to ever play a nazi hence he doesnt fall into the typical traps of a stale nazi perfromance, here its just .... cristoph waltz reincarnation!AU samuel l jackson had an absolutely insane performance, see again, he could have gone for the easy minstrel, i mean thats basically his character, yet he felt genuinely contorted himself into his own unique antagonist, basically what waltz did in inglorious anyways , kinda crap, still worth watching, interesting premise i guess? texto: As a black female adult, I’ve come to realization that I hated  this movie solely because how Quentin Tarantino portrays the  whole concept of a enslaved man became free based on a white bounty hunter and helped him kill different slave masters. The whole movie didn’t sit right with me. To be honest, as a southern black woman herself it made my blood boiled. I had to cut the movie off halfway when I saw the scene of two black man fighting to the death for their slave master as a betting deal and entertainment. I understand he was trying to get the concept of how it was back than but I felt that it was unnecessary that every sentence or dialogue was n***a this and n***a that. An a white man directing a ‘black slave movie’ showing the different trademarks of how black people was treated, punished, and abused doesn’t sit right. Basically showing it from a white point of view than black point of view. There’s a difference. I didn’t feel educated not one bit to how my ancestors were treated back than. I used to love this as kid but as I became older I realized that this movie is disrespectful towards black people and I stand by that.

exemplo: Este grupo critica o uso exagerado de sangue e cenas violentas, considerando-as irrealistas e cansativas, embora algumas reconheçam que isso faz parte do estilo do diretor.
texto: Um breve comentário... Revisitando "Django", descobri que possuo uma série de incômodos com esse filme. Não consigo afirmar que é um filme ruim, muito menos que é brilhante. Mas há algo aqui que me incomoda profundamente. E acredito ser a maneira como Tarantino dirige sua violência. Não sua eloquência estética que jorra para todos os lados. Mas as escolhas feitas para a construção do ódio sobre os donos de escravos. Em "Bastardos Inglórios", Tarantino não precisa recorrer aos atos de barbárie da segunda guerra para construir a imagem dos nazistas ou alocar a faixa de "esses são os vilões". Pelo contrário, os atos de barbárie apenas recaem sobre eles (com exceção da introdução de Shosanna), e assim somos levados por toda a história. Mas, aqui? Existe um tratamento com o corpo negro que me causa náuseas. Não só a colocação de Django, em alguns momentos, como um sujeito inocente, infantil, incapaz e que precisa de tutela, mas as introduções de Broomhilda serem sempre pautadas pela transgressão de seu corpo. Sua personagem é uma passageira da agonia frente aos nossos olhos. E aí, o tratamento de ventríloquo que Tarantino dar a seus personagens prejudica a própria substância que os constitui. Broomhilda é apenas uma boneca que está sendo torturada durante todo o filme. Apenas esperando a morte ou a surpresa de seu salvador. É engraçado esse filme vir logo após bastardos. Principalmente pelas decisões tomadas de reconstruir cenas de violência ao corpo negro, quase que com o intuito de fazer com quem o telespectador compre a ideia que o dono de escravos é o "homem mal". Como se ser DONOS DE ESCRAVOS já não fossem suficiente, da mesma maneira que ser nazista. Não falo se a escolha do diretor é certa ou errado, se devia ou não estar ali, mas das sensações que provoca ao telespectador. E sim, acho engraçado que em um filme ele não recorra a barbárie ao povo judeu, mas a corpos negros ele dedica tanto tempo e estilo para isso. Sim, DiCaprio rouba o filme pra si. Sim, a sequência de sua morte e o show de sangue é catártico, como muitos filmes de Tarantino NÃO conseguem ser. Mas até chegarmos a esse ponto, somos levados a uma exploração da violência sobre o corpo negro que me causa náuseas.

texto: I think this is just not for me, even on a rewatch I think while there are undeniably great aspects to this film its just so messy as a whole I struggle to get behind anything it puts down. The performances here are probably the biggest detractor, aside from Walz they lack any sort of finesse or styling they are just these over-acted messes I think Leo is the biggest casuality here, Candy at his core feels like he could be a great character but because of Dicaprio's one note performance his character misses any nuance or any quality that would make it stick in my mind for any amount of time. Jamie Foxx feels similarly shallow offering nothing but an attempt at a commanding presence that never feels all that intimidating or striking, and SLJ just kind of flails around. I think because I'm such a huge western fan this one would've have been really special to make it in for me but Tarantino's hodge podge just feels unbalanced insensitive and unfunny. It feels more like a parody of the genre without any understanding what makes the tropes of the genre interesting. Focusing more on reference value and showing the viewer that it is in fact a western than creating something more a cheap roller-coaster ride that certainly has some highs but also makes me reach for the paper bag more than once. The way the film tries to make any sort of a message is baffling to me. Its as if Tarantino got out a balancing scale and was like if I put in loads of goofy and comedic elements but mix it in with loads of edgy, "cool" and violent moments it'll somehow balance out, but to me it just feels disjointed. The film tries to balance the racism it explores with no accountability, there is no justice for D'artagnan just a fuckload of n-slurs. And while the oppressors are brought to justice by the end the way its just handled with zero weight or magnitude makes it all feel worthless by the end. That being said I believe the film really has some fantastic scenes in isolation, the scene where Django shoots his first bounty with Schulz or the one where they're at the dinner table in candy land are still genuinely tense and the opening is really fun, but it's overall tonal dissonance and general feeling of lack of weight make this a dud for me. Not bad just not for me.

texto: Um breve comentário... Revisitando "Django", descobri que possuo uma série de incômodos com esse filme. Não consigo afirmar que é um filme ruim, muito menos que é brilhante. Mas há algo aqui que me incomoda profundamente. E acredito ser a maneira como Tarantino dirige sua violência. Não sua eloquência estética que jorra para todos os lados. Mas as escolhas feitas para a construção do ódio sobre os donos de escravos. Em "Bastardos Inglórios", Tarantino não precisa recorrer aos atos de barbárie da segunda guerra para construir a imagem dos nazistas ou alocar a faixa de "esses são os vilões". Pelo contrário, os atos de barbárie apenas recaem sobre eles (com exceção da introdução de Shosanna), e assim somos levados por toda a história. Mas, aqui? Existe um tratamento com o corpo negro que me causa náuseas. Não só a colocação de Django, em alguns momentos, como um sujeito inocente, infantil, incapaz e que precisa de tutela, mas as introduções de Broomhilda serem sempre pautadas pela transgressão de seu corpo. Sua personagem é uma passageira da agonia frente aos nossos olhos. E aí, o tratamento de ventríloquo que Tarantino dar a seus personagens prejudica a própria substância que os constitui. Broomhilda é apenas uma boneca que está sendo torturada durante todo o filme. Apenas esperando a morte ou a surpresa de seu salvador. É engraçado esse filme vir logo após bastardos. Principalmente pelas decisões tomadas de reconstruir cenas de violência ao corpo negro, quase que com o intuito de fazer com quem o telespectador compre a ideia que o dono de escravos é o "homem mal". Como se ser DONOS DE ESCRAVOS já não fossem suficiente, da mesma maneira que ser nazista. Não falo se a escolha do diretor é certa ou errado, se devia ou não estar ali, mas das sensações que provoca ao telespectador. E sim, acho engraçado que em um filme ele não recorra a barbárie ao povo judeu, mas a corpos negros ele dedica tanto tempo e estilo para isso. Sim, DiCaprio rouba o filme pra si. Sim, a sequência de sua morte e o show de sangue é catártico, como muitos filmes de Tarantino NÃO conseguem ser. Mas até chegarmos a esse ponto, somos levados a uma exploração da violência sobre o corpo negro que me causa náuseas.

texto: Decided to rewatch this after recently watching the original (1966) Django. I first watched this with my family when it came out, so over 10 years ago now. I also wanted to see if my opinion on it would change. Well, my thoughts on it are about the same. I think this is a fine / decent film, but not nearly as great as everyone else seems to think. Possibly a hot take, but I actually slightly prefer the original Django. Sure, there's no doubt Unchained has better acting, better budget and production, a star studded cast, etc. - but it's also a bit padded out and long winded, indulgent, and... I don't know. Something about it feels a bit contrived and artificial. I absolutely loved Inglorious Basterds, which shares many similarities to this; it's a soft remake of an earlier action/exploitation movie, but in that case I think it far exceeds its source material, with a much more convincing story and emotional ties to the characters. Unchained, at least for me, just doesn't quite have that. Again, a decent movie but it's not one I love. I prefer the leaner and grittier original film. It was cool, though, seeing the cameos this time that I hadn't noticed before. (Franco Nero, Tom Savini, John Jarrat)

texto: Que FILMAÇO! Meu primeiro filme do Tarantino e, cara, é tanta coisa, tantas mensagens que te pegam. Uma hora esse filme te faz sentir raiva, outra hora você ri, outra hora fica eufórico. E, nossa, quantas sensações diferentes em um filme de faroeste. Quanto a uma crítica, não vou tentar me estender muito, mas esse filme facilmente daria uns 20 parágrafos. Bom, o filme é dividido em três arcos muito bem definidos, e eu gostei bastante dessa divisão. É bem explícita a ascensão do Django, a missão para resgatar a Brunilda e, por fim, o clímax. Cada uma dessas partes é muito divertida e cheia de críticas à época da escravidão, ao tratamento dado aos negros, ao racismo e etc. Todas essas críticas são ridiculamente bem escritas e cirúrgicas, justamente por serem secas e te deixarem com raiva daquilo que está sendo mostrado (ou, pelo menos, é isso que deveria acontecer). Ao mesmo tempo, em alguns momentos você consegue rir da situação, seja pelo absurdo, seja pela graça mesmo. As atuações são estupendas. Os três atores principais roubam a cena: Jamie Foxx, Christoph Waltz e Leonardo DiCaprio. Principalmente o DiCaprio. Minha nossa, que vilão bom. Ele é acompanhado por um subvilão, interpretado pelo Samuel L. Jackson, que a todo momento consegue te deixar com raiva. Minha nossa, que raiva desse personagem. O Waltz e o Jamie Foxx também têm uma química que funciona desde o minuto 1 do filme. Os dois são muito bons juntos e conseguem carregar boa parte da história com uma naturalidade absurda. Uma coisa que achei muito interessante foi a evolução do Django. Graças ao roteiro, é perceptível o desenvolvimento dele por meio do letramento e do pensamento individual. É muito satisfatório acompanhar isso e ver como o personagem vai mudando ao longo do filme. A cena da KKK, de longe, é uma das coisas mais engraçadas do filme. É tão idiota que acaba sendo genial, e a cena termina de uma forma espetacular. Pra terminar, só apontar a única (única mesmo) coisa que não gostei: o ritmo do começo. A diferença de ritmo entre o primeiro terço do filme e o momento em que eles conhecem o personagem do DiCaprio fez com que o início demorasse um pouco pra mim. Mas talvez seja só meu cérebro derretido pelo TikTok, enfim, fica aí o comentário. Que filme maravilhoso. Fica a dica.

texto: Went a little out of order in Tarantino’s filmography because I couldn’t wait anymore to finally watch this again, and it’s easily my favorite out of what I’ve watched/rewatched so far. Everything about it is so unforgettable: the dialogue, the shootouts, performances (every single person in this movie contributing massively to the finished product), and the sets. All of the plantations feel as massive as they’re supposed to and each with their own unique parts to them. I love Christoph Waltz so much and can’t wait to watch Inglorious Basterds again too.

texto: Django is insanely tuff Quentin Tarantino did it again. He just knows how to make movies. The cast is as always goated asf. Probably top 10 soundtracks ever. Everything is just perfect like always. You know a movie is good when you don’t have much too say and it’s somehow always Quentin Tarantino that makes this possible. Everyone’s performance was at his personal peak. I’ve never seen Leonardo Di Caprio act that way ever and he’s part of the movie that makes it unforgettable. That also counts for Christoph Waltz my german goat! Ugh how I love him 😫🙌🏼 I love that he always voices himself in German and that we can hear his insane beautiful voice that he has.
